prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B024 alone, credited to Katori and Ye. Having read all eight statements, I find that no one disputes the quality of the result, only its novelty relative to 2005 and 2012, its timing and its credit at the edges, so I will answer those directly. On novelty: the comb gave a way to count optical cycles and the 2012 prize honoured control of one isolated quantum system. The lattice clock is a different physical regime. Magic-wavelength trapping cancels the differential light shift while many atoms sit in the Lamb-Dicke regime, free of Doppler and recoil shifts, so one gets single-ion-like systematics together with the signal-to-noise of an ensemble. That statistical advantage, not the comb, is what moved stability and accuracy to the 10^-18 range, and it is what opened clock comparisons at the level of gravitational redshift over centimetres, tighter limits on drifting constants and many-body effects in a clock. I would put this distinction in the citation wording rather than leave it implicit, as Kroll suggests, and I have therefore included the magic-wavelength mechanism in the citation. On credit: Katori proposed the scheme and demonstrated the first lattice clock, and Ye's group took it to record accuracy and added the Fermi-degenerate, many-body regime. Two names is a judgment, but it follows the invention and the demonstration of its decisive performance. This is a closer call than my round-1 text suggested, and I hold it on the physics rather than on the count of first places.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains attribution. Lemonde, Sterr, Hollberg, the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups and the ion-clock programmes contributed to the field, and a two-name prize leaves them out. Olsson's question whether Ye is credited for co-invention or realization is fair: my reading is realization of record performance plus the many-body extension, not the original proposal, and the citation should say 'invention and realization' only because the pair together cover both. The second objection is that the lineage comb, ion, lattice may look like a third prize for one tradition. I think the physics answers it, but a colleague who weighs discovery of a new state of matter above a new measurement capability will not be moved by my argument, and Pearce is right that B003 has the stronger claim to open a new field. Finally, the redefinition of the second remains outstanding. I still consider it irrelevant to the discovery, but I accept that this is a view about the criteria, not a fact.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B003 because it is a prediction followed by a surprising discovery, is the widest common ground (six of eight in the top three), and sees B024 as the more mature but less novel option; he accepts B024 if the moire interpretation is judged immature.
responses.response: I agree that B003 is the strongest condensed-matter case on the list and I ranked it second. The 2011 prediction followed by the 2018 observation at the predicted angle is a clean sequence. Where we differ is on how much interpretive maturity a prize needs. I would want the citation to rest only on flat bands and correlated states, and I note that you and Danielsson both concede the pairing mechanism and the dependence on twist-angle disorder are unsettled. That is a real difference from B024, where the measurement and its uncertainty budget are independently reproduced. Evidence that would move me toward B003 is a resolved pairing picture or a consensus on which of the correlated phases are intrinsic. I also do not think wide second-choice support settles anything: it shows B003 is respected, not that it is ripe. I would not regard a B003 prize as an error, and I would support it as the fallback if B024 stalls.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B003 as a discovery in nature, calls B024 the safe and defensible alternative, and notes that high-temperature superconductors were recognised before their mechanism was understood.
responses.response: The cuprate precedent is a fair one and I do not claim that mechanism is a prerequisite. The difference I see is that cuprate superconductivity was a robust, reproducible and enormous change in a measurable property, while in twisted graphene sample-to-sample variation still makes the phase diagram contested between laboratories. 'Safe' also undersells B024 a little: a record-accuracy atomic clock is not a safe choice in scientific terms, it is the result with the sharpest quantitative test. I accept your point on credit more than I did in round 1. The omission of Yuan Cao and the Dean, Young and Yazdani experiments is a heavier problem for B003 than the omitted clock groups are for B024, because there the omitted names sit on the central discovery rather than on supporting technique.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, supports B024 but warns that a clock prize may be read as an instrument achievement rather than a discovery, and that an unfavourable reading would treat the SI redefinition as the formal consummation.
responses.response: I take the instrument objection seriously, and it is the best argument against my own choice. My answer is that the lattice clock was not only an instrument: it brought a new regime of physics, many atoms with cancelled light shift, and the clocks are now themselves the experiments, bounding variation of constants and measuring gravitational potential differences. On the redefinition, the Committee is rewarding the demonstrated result, and a unit's adoption is decided by metrology bodies on grounds that are partly administrative. If waiting for it is the committee's wish, I would say so in discussion, but I would not treat it as a scientific criterion. I agree with you that B003 and B023 carry a stronger claim to open new fields, and I would not argue that B024 does that in the same way.

responses.point: Kroll supports B024, asks that the citation state why the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and discloses a doctoral research stay in John Hall's Boulder laboratory.
responses.response: I agree with the drafting point and have adopted it. On the Boulder disclosure, the chair summary groups Kroll and me together as having a Boulder connection linked to the comb prize. That is not accurate for me. I have no documented research stay there. My documented connections are to the Lund attosecond group, Keller's group and L'Huillier. I do not think Kroll's earlier stay requires recusal, because Hall's honoured work is the 2005 comb and the boundary question is a scientific one that Kroll is well placed to discuss; but I would ask the committee to state this explicitly so that the record is clear.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B006 on active matter as a new conceptual class, but states that quantitative confirmation of the Toner-Tu exponents is weak and that B024 is stronger if a sharp measurable outcome is the test.
responses.response: I appreciate that Mehlig states the weakness of his own ballot plainly. The conceptual point is real: long-range order in two dimensions in a non-equilibrium system, in the face of Mermin-Wagner, is a surprising result. My reservation matches his own, that the quantitative scaling is only partly confirmed and the three-name cut leaves out Marchetti, Cates, Simha and Chate. I do not think the committee needs a measurable outcome from every candidate in the same sense, but for a result still being tested after thirty years I would want the experimental confirmation of the exponents before awarding it. I would not put B006 among my alternatives for this round.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts lattice clocks as distinct from the comb and ion-control prizes; I believe so but it rests on a physics argument that others must find convincing.
Whether two names fairly represent the lattice-clock community given Lemonde, Sterr, Hollberg and the ion-clock leaders; I have not independently verified priority details.
Whether the committee will wait for the redefinition of the second, which I consider scientifically irrelevant but which others may weigh.
Whether discovery of a new phase of matter (B003) should outweigh a new measurement regime (B024) for those who ranked B003 first; this is a difference in criteria that I cannot settle with evidence.
My knowledge of the literature comes from memory, not from checking original papers during this simulation.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: my profile documents collaboration with Anne L'Huillier, papers with the Lund attosecond group, collaboration with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and work with Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato. None of this is documented as a tie to Katori, Ye or the other clock groups, so I see no specific conflict for B024, B003 or B014. My field of atomic theory is adjacent to precision spectroscopy, so I may overrate the importance of the atomic-structure problems in B024 and I discount my judgment on condensed-matter candidates. I have no Boulder research stay; that point in the chair's summary applies to Kroll alone.
